pass_rule: all core questions substantially correct in the learner's own words; stretch questions inform the grade, not the gate

questions.prompt: Name the three letters of the GMP model and what each one is. Then tell the whole story of a goroutine entering a blocking syscall — from the moment the thread enters the kernel to the moment the goroutine runs Go code again.
expected_points: G = goroutine (small stack + state), M = OS thread, P = scheduling token holding a local run queue; running Go code requires all three
the M is trapped in the kernel with its G; sysmon notices and detaches the P
the P is handed to another M (woken or newly created) so other goroutines keep running
on return the M needs a P; if none is free the G goes to the global run queue and the M parks

questions.prompt: GOMAXPROCS=1 and you start 100,000 goroutines. Is that a contradiction? Explain what GOMAXPROCS actually bounds, and how work stealing fits into the picture when GOMAXPROCS is larger.
expected_points: no contradiction: GOMAXPROCS is the number of Ps — simultaneous execution slots — not a limit on goroutines
parallelism (running at the same instant) is bounded; concurrency (in-flight, interleaved goroutines) is not
an idle P's M, after checking the global queue and netpoller, steals half of another P's local run queue
stealing is why goroutines spawned in one place spread across all Ps without any placement by the programmer

questions.prompt: A goroutine runs `for { x++ }` — no function calls. Before Go 1.14 this could freeze a program; today it can't. Explain both preemption mechanisms and why the old one failed here, plus why this bug was worse than mere unfairness.
expected_points: cooperative preemption reuses the stack-bound check in function prologues — the runtime poisons the bound so the next call reschedules
a call-free loop never hits a prologue check, so it could hold its P forever
since Go 1.14 sysmon sends a signal (SIGURG) to a G running ~10ms+, suspending it at nearly any instruction
GC begins with stop-the-world, so one unpreemptible loop could stall garbage collection and thus the whole program

questions.prompt: Roughly what does a new goroutine cost, what happens when it outgrows its stack, and when is goroutine-per-request the right design versus when would you bound goroutine creation?
expected_points: ~2 KiB initial stack (runtime-adaptive) plus a small descriptor — versus megabytes for an OS thread
stacks grow by allocating a larger stack and copying, transparently, up to a large cap; they can shrink at GC
per-request is right when goroutines mostly park on runtime/netpoller waits and hold little — the net/http model
bound (worker pool / semaphore channel) when each goroutine holds scarce resources, blocks a thread in syscalls/cgo, or spawning is unbounded by any upstream limit

questions.prompt: A service on 8 cores shows latency spikes; schedtrace reports threads climbing past 1,000 while gomaxprocs=8 and all run queues sit near zero. What is happening, what evidence would you collect, and name one fix?
expected_points: thread growth with empty run queues points at goroutines blocking OS threads in syscalls or cgo — not CPU starvation
each simultaneously blocking call traps an M and forces the runtime to back-fill with new threads; the 10k-thread limit eventually kills the process
evidence: execution trace showing Gs in syscall state, a threadcreate profile, or bisecting the recent dependency change
fix: bound the blocking calls with a semaphore/worker pool, or replace the blocking API with a pollable / pure-Go alternative — raising GOMAXPROCS is not a fix

questions.prompt: Play language designer: goroutines and threads seem sufficient — why did Go add the P at all?
expected_points: P cleanly bounds parallelism at GOMAXPROCS regardless of how many threads exist
one-owner Ps make local run queues lock-free; a single global locked queue was the old design and didn't scale across cores
Ps carry per-P caches (e.g. allocator caches), avoiding cross-thread contention

questions.prompt: Three goroutines block: one in time.Sleep, one reading an idle TCP socket, one in a raw blocking read(2) on a pipe. How many OS threads do the three of them tie up, and why is each case different?
expected_points: sleep: zero threads — the runtime's timer machinery parks the G
socket: zero threads — the netpoller registers the fd (epoll/kqueue) and parks the G until readiness
raw syscall: one whole thread — the M is trapped in the kernel and its P is handed off
the asymmetry is why goroutine-per-connection servers scale but syscall/cgo-heavy workloads need bounding
